The resolution passed in the house prior to the introduction of the bill proposed to extend to March 31, 1941, the period during which payment shall be made of arrears or instalments due and payable between March 31, 1933 and March 31, 1938. The amendment proposes to add three years beyond 1938 to the period during which these arrears and instalments have become payable. The amendment, therefore, imposes a new charge upon the treasury.
When the resolution is framed in general terms there is no limitation on the amount authorized by the crown's recommendation; but in this case the resolution limits the period during which arrears and instalments have become payable, namely, from April, 1933, to April, 1938. This limitation cannot be extended by this committee. The hon. member who moved the amendment quoted from May. If he will turn to May's Parliamentary Practice, page 510, he will find that the application of the provisions of a bill may be extended-

so long as the power conferred by the royal recommendation is not exceeded.
The amendment proposes to exceed this power, and, if it should carry, the liability of the government would be increased, which would mean a charge upon the people. For these reasons the amendment is out of order.

subtopic: INTEREST RATE ON REPAYMENTS OF TAXES AND INSURANCE PREMIUMS-ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
I have the very highest
respect, Mr. Chairman, for your office and for yourself, and while I have no regrets so far as I am personally concerned, I do regret to see that all the authorities have been ignored. Bourinot, May, and even the leader of the opposition have turned your decision down. Owing to my respect for yourself and your office I shall not delay the committee by challenging your decision, but I am sorry to say that truth compels me to state that I think you are wrong. That point being disposed of, I shall now get back to the original principle of the bill with regard to which I wish to present some argument that may yet, I fondly hope, influence the minister to take a different attitude.
I wish to quote from a resolution passed by the Soldier Settlers' Union. There is a provincial executive in Saskatchewan, one in Alberta and a headquarters executive, and
this organization passed the following resolution dated March 6, 1938. It is not addressed to anyone in particular. It reads:
Dear Sir:
I have been instructed to protest vigorously by the executive of the Soldier Settlers' Union on behalf of its more than 2,000 members, the bill placed before the House of Commons by the Hon. T. A. Crerar to continue the dollar for dollar legislation based on the recommendations of the Legion dominion convention held recently at Fort William.
This convention was certainly not representative of the soldier settlers of the western provinces. The examination of the many resolutions passed by locals of the Legion in the west will prove that no consideration could have been given to the voice of the soldier settler of the west.
Further evidence of this is provided by the fact that at the 1936 dominion convention of the Legion held at Vancouver at which soldier settlers were able to send representation, the convention unanimously passed a far different resolution calling for:-Revaluation at present day values and the cancellation of interest charges retroactive to the commencement of the loan.
We contend that this complete about face was due to the fact that soldier settlers were able to be represented at the western convention but because of financial difficulties were unable to be represented at the recent convention of the Legion held in eastern Canada.
Furthermore, why should the recommendations of the Soldier Settlers' Union which was recognized as an organization officially by the government by our inclusion in the conference of 1933, be excluded and the recommendations of a convention which was not by any means representative of the majority of settlers be accepted and acted upon in such feverish haste. This action in the face of the minister's statement to our organization contained in his letter dated February 25, 1937, promising full consideration to the representations of soldier organizations is very difficult to understand.
We strongly urge that a conference be arranged to bring about a permanent solution to the settlement problem or that a referendum be taken among the settlers ami the public to decide this question.
That was an unsolieited letter which came to me. I have also a statement, unsolicited- I was in ignorance of it-drawn up by a man calling himself a zone representative, Mr. A. S. Cobum of Nanaimo, a man of standing and reputation in his town. He lives about one hundred miles from where the settlers I represent live-I am not referring to the settlers to whom the resolution I have just quoted refers. This gentleman went there of his own accord last November and on his return submitted a report to the soldiers' legion. I have a letter from a Mr. Payne acknowled-, ging receipt of it; therefore I assume he handed it to the head of the legion, and it
Soldier Settlement Act

did or should have formed a part of the representations he made to the minister. And we find the minister stating that he had a lengthy conversation with the president, satisfying himself that his present legislation was in accordance with the wishes of the convention. Let me read what this zone official says: It is rather a long communication; but it is very important to the people I represent, and if it is the last thing I do in this parliament I shall put it on the record:
On the 3rd November, I visited the Comox valley to investigate the various reports on the plight and hardships of the soldier settlers. It is my intent to present facts pertaining to these men and some of the reasons why their payments of principal, interest and taxes could not be met.
For some time past their position has been steadily growing worse, and the time has now arrived when some immediate and remedial action must be taken. The statements and figures following cannot be challenged. During the period 1919-1921, when returned men settled in this area, a number of them were advised to enter the poultry business. It may have been considered good advice, but events have proved otherwise.
In 1919, the winter price of eggs was over $1 per dozen, and in March, 1920, the low price was 50 cents per dozen. In May, 1932, the low price was 6 cents per dozen, and the average price for the spring and summer months was 7 cents. On November 28 of that year the high price was 22 cents and by November 5, it had dropped to 15 cents per dozen. Men carrying flocks from 1,500 to 2,000 birds, were either forced out of business or were obliged to reduce their flocks to 150 or 200 birds. Many feed bills have been owing from that time until the present. The names of these men can be supplied at any time.
I can personally endorse that because I was in the feed business in those years, and in the place where I lived I had to write off many a poultry bill.
The decline in egg prices was fairly steady from 1919 to 1932, but the cost of production was seldom under 18 cents per dozen, and for a considerable period well in excess of that figure.
During 1919-20 others were advised to enter the dairy business. At that time cows cost around $175 to $200 each. A condensery was started at Courtenay and it was pointed out that European countries would purchase an unlimited supply of this product. It was found, however, that condensed milk was produced to such an extent in foreign countries that there was a considerable surplus, with the result that the condensery closed down in 1920, and in 1921 the price of cows dropped to $35 and $40, thereby entailing a serious loss to those entering this business. Since 1930 a considerable number of sales have taken place in the Comox valley and a large number of dairy cows have sold as low as $10 and $15 each. Some have sold this fall as low as $15.
[Mr. Neill.j
In 1920 in the month of February the condensery paid 85 cents per pound for butter fat, and the lowest price for that year was 60 cents per pound. In 1932 the highest price was 28 cents and the lowest was 17 cents per pound. For 1937 it has ranged from 28 to 32 cents. Arguments have been put forward that the cost of production is lower. It may be quoted here that the price of bran in February, 1920, was $2.35 per hundred pounds, and in April, 1937, it was $2.25, a difference of only 10 cents, but a difference in butter fat of 53 cents per pound.
In 1920 pork was 23 cents per pound, live weight. In 1933 it dropped to 4 cents per pound. Six weeks old pigs were $10 each in December, 1920. In November 8, 1933, they were purchased for $2 each. In February, 1920, veal was worth 23 cents per pound, and in 1933 the best price obtainable was 9 cents.
I questioned one settler regarding the growing of potatoes. He stated that in the spring of 1920 he had purchased seed from a neighbour, paying for 900 pounds at the rate of $180 per ton. In 1920 he grew thirty-five acres at a cost of $3,500. A portion of the crop was sold at from $10 to $14 per ton below the cost of production, and over a hundred tons were dumped as it was impossible to market them at any price. The loss sustained was in the neighbourhood of $2,500.
Market gardening has been followed by some of the settlers, but the cost of production is in excess of the selling price, mainly owing to oriental competition and the scarcity of reliable help.
Fruit growing has not been carried on, mainly owing to soil and climatic conditions, and the lack of satisfactory markets, which are very limited.
The prices quoted above have been taken from settlers' accounts, and are not quoted from memory. They can be verified.
Summing up the situation in this district, it would appear that a number of problems face these men. It must be remembered that at the time of purchase, from the figures quoted they had reason to believe they had a fair chance to make payments, and undoubtedly would have done so but that conditions (which it must be admitted were world wide) were against them. Prices dropped in the ease of many farm products to one-fifth of the prices obtainable at the time of purchase.
Prices of land in 1919 and 1920 were considerably in excess of its productive value. It is conceded that certain reductions have been made by the government, but this is not enough. Some of the loans, through no fault of the settlers, are now up to where they were before the thirty per cent reduction was made. This is owing to the continual piling up of interest. The value of farm land is extremely low at the present time. Some of the best land in the Comox valley, namely, part of the old Lewis estate, sold recently for $50 per acre. This is rich cleared land, and preferably to any land in the valley. Compare this with land purchased for the settlers at $100 to $150 per acre. It might be mentioned here also that a large percentage of this land had been cropped out before the men bought it.
Local conditions militate against these men. The Comox valley is the centre of an extensive logging industry, and the minimum wage in

Soldier Settlement Act
these camps is $4.20 per day. All fit young men are working in the bush, and it is natural that they prefer that to working (at wages far below those quoted) on the farm.
Considerable difficulty has been experienced in marketing potatoes in Victoria. In spite of the fact that the quality of potatoes grown in the valley is equal to that of any part of the province, the wholesalers are not giving Comox an even break. This is probably due to the request made at the time of the Stevens price spreads commission to have these firms investigated. As an instance of this attitude, recently the agent of the control board ordered two cars from the valley at a price of $24 per ton f.o.b. Victoria. The local agent of the board canvassed the growers and arranged for the quantity ordered. One car was loaded and word was received from the agent at Victoria cancelling the other car and stating that the price of the first car had dropped to $21 . . . unfair treatment has been handed out to these men for a number of years and many instances cqn be quoted.
In the early days of settlement large quantities of pork were purchased by the orientals working in the Cumberland mines. Since that time the company has eliminated Chinamen a^id for some time it has been extremely hard to market this product.
Having set forth in the foregoing paragraphs some of the reasons for losses entailed and non-payment of the amounts due, and after having given very careful consideration to this matter, I feel that if these men are to stay on the land some action must be taken by the government immediately. It must be remembered that these men who fought for Canada in the dark days of 1914-18 are aging fast, trying to make a home, which they feel will never belong to them and which, when they pass on, their widow and childrent must evacuate to make room for aliens, who should certainly not be given preference to the dependents of returned men.
The dollar for dollar arrangement has not proved of much benefit to the original settler, as he has not had the money to take advantage with. It has benefited those in receipt of pensions, high wages, or private means. The men who are honestly trying to make a living from the land have been unable to take advantage of it. If the government had offered $5 instead of $1 it is doubtful if a cent more would have been paid.
The board has advised a number of these men to take their cases before the farmers' creditors arrangement board. It does not seem right that they should be treated as bankrupts. The board argues this is not the case, but the settlers do not agree with this argument. Their credit is gone when this action is taken.
It would appear to me that all interest must be cancelled on loans, and this should be retroactive to the date of the thirty per cent reduction. This is not asking the government to create a precedent, as they loaned the Canadian Pacific Railway many millions of dollars, free of interest. Surely the returned men are entitled to equal consideration.
Some of the settlers would like to dispose of a portion of their holdings, and I suggest the government take over such portions at a valuation agreeable to the settler, or arrived a>t by arbitration. This would materially reduce many of the loans.
It is important that action must be taken immediately. Many of these men have sacrificed themselves and their families enough. They have gone short of food and clothes trying to carry on. Their morale is low, and the worry is becoming too much for them.
It is distinctly understood that any remedial legislation should apply only to original settlers.
Now the man who makes that report is this Mr. A. S. Coburn, who does not live in the district, who has no personal or business interest there; his business is not one which would lead him to deal with these settlers in any way; he is an utterly unbiased man coming into the district because he felt it his duty as the zone representative of the Canadian legion. This is not my language, but his, although I can endorse every word from personal experience and knowledge. That is his plea, in order to allow me to ask that this amelioration which the minister proposes should be widened to the extent at least that we thought was intended in the resolution. I shall not go into that again; we shall accept the situation as the minister states it. But on the bare merits of the thing, can he not see his way to extend it as I indicated in the amendment which was turned down? The cost would not be a great deal, because, as the leader of the opposition pointed out the other day, you would probably get more money in if you grant this; for otherwise the men will be in despair; they will say, "Take your land; I cannot make anything of it; I would rather go out, and we might as well go now as five years hence." But if you made this reduction it would encourage them to go on, and would be a very different matter.
There was placed in our hands the other day the report of the soldier settlement board. I take some facts out of it. Only 7-1 per cent of the instalments due or in arrears on October 1 last in British Columbia were paid. At that rate, how many years will it take the settlers to catch up on the arrears, plus the amount falling due each year for instalments and compound interest? Take the total collections for the year, including the British families scheme; the cost of collection works out at fifty per cent of the total collected. In other words, the government is going to collect this money, if they can get it, and it is going to cost them fifty cents on the dollar to collect it. Why not let the settlers keep it and stay on the land? I think that is a very strong point. You are not going to get this money anyway; so why not make a gesture and let the settlers stay on the land? If you throw them off, you will resell the land at an enormous reduction and somebody else, possibly an alien, will reap the benefit.
Soldier Settlement Act

I recall a farm quite close to where I live. I have worked on it, and am quite familiar with it. Some years ago the board turned out the settler and offered the farm for sale. I suggested that they sell it to a man whom I would produce, for SI,200 or $1,300, but they said no; they wanted $3,000. I said, "Yes, possibly you will sell it for that, but you will not get the $3,000. You will only have the land back again in a year or two." They said they were going to sell it for $3,000, but 1 said, "If you will sell it for $1,300 you will get that amount in cash, and that will end it." What happened? They did get a man to buy it for $3,000 on time. He went broke, and they took the land away from him. They sold it to another man for something like $2,000, but he went broke and they took it back again. Now they are hawking it around at the price I suggested six or eight years ago. What has that system of management profited them? I am not pleading altogether for the settlers, though their situation is bad enough; I am speaking in the interests of economy and getting rid of this system of paying out fifty cents in expenses to get a dollar. We should make some settlement. It is not as though this were confined to the government alone; I am told that a large number of mortgage companies in the west are making the same offer to people indebted to them. They know it is better to get something than to get nothing, and that is the point I want to impress upon the minister.
I shall not delay the committee longer. I have put the case to the best of my poor ability, and I only wish I were more eloquent. If I could only get the minister out there so that he could see these things for himself, I am convinced that he would make a change in this legislation.

subtopic: INTEREST RATE ON REPAYMENTS OF TAXES AND INSURANCE PREMIUMS-ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
I rise to protest once more against these amendments passing, and I must say that I am disappointed at the lack of any proper excuse given by the government for the introduction of this measure I listened carefully to the remarks of the minister both at the time he introduced the bill and during this debate, and one statement which he made stands out in my memory. I am going to endeavour to correct it as far as British Columbia is concerned. I refer to his statement with regard to agricultural prices.
It would appear that there are two motives for these amendments. One must be an endeavour to have those pay up who so far have not done so. The second probably is to save the government money. With regard

to the first motive, when I look at the statement given me by the officials of the department I am at a loss to understand just how the settlers who have not paid possibly can make a rush now to make payment, in view of the fact that this legislation has been in existence for some three years, and many of them have been unable to make any payments at all. It is not that they are unwilling to make their payments. They would be only too willing to do so if they had the funds; but, as I pointed out, with eggs at seventeen cents a dozen, with potatoes they cannot sell, with hay they gave away and with the clearing of land as difficult as it is in the Fraser valley, it is impossible for these soldier settlers to make any payments whatever.
If the minister thinks that by this amendment he is going to save money, I should like to point out to him that out of a total of 1,668 settlers who should have made payments last year, only some 475 paid in full. There are thirteen districts in British Columbia, each with a supervisor. It will cost at least $50,000 to pay those supervisors, in addition to the cost of keeping up that office in which, as can be readily seen if anyone cares to visit it, many people are given employment. But if they collected only S100,294 in all last year, when the bonus for bonus system was in effect, with 475 settlers making full payment and 529 making partial payments, it would seem to me that under this plan the government are going to lose money. They are going to keep thirteen supervisors at work, together with the head office staff, with no returns whatever. So this cannot be defended on the score that they are going to save money. If the idea is to induce those who have not paid during the last few years to pay up, I say it will not make them do any such thing, because under the extremely difficult economic conditions prevailing in British Columbia they simply cannot do so.
I mentioned that before, but I took note that the minister made no reply. When he spoke of the increased agricultural prices he may have been referring to the prairie provinces, probably to Saskatchewan, but I am speaking particularly of the lower Fraser valley. I say to him that if he puts through this amendment there will be very little money taken in; yet it will cost almost $100,000 to maintain the office and the thirteen supervisors in British Columbia. I say it is impossible for the settlers to pay. Many of them, if not all, are excellent settlers, but they have not had a chance to make any payments. They have this grievance. While it is true that many reductions have been made by way of bonus, revaluation of land

Soldier Settlement Act
and so on, the fact still remains that to-day there are on the land civilian settlers who obtained that land under the soldier settlement board for a quarter of the valuation which is assessed against the soldier settlers.

subtopic: INTEREST RATE ON REPAYMENTS OF TAXES AND INSURANCE PREMIUMS-ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
Yes, the present value; not the previous value. I have a case in point, concerning two pieces of property near my own home. The soldier settler there is paying at the rate of S50 an acre to-day, after the revaluation and all the other reductions. Close to him there was another soldier settler who sold out some three years ago. That land was sold for $10 an acre, so that a civilian paying $10 an acre is living alongside an original soldier settler who is assessed $50 an acre. That soldier settler has been unable to take advantage of this plan, and in that he is only one of many hundreds throughout the Eraser valley.
A voice says, " Why didn't he come under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act?" That has been exploded time and again in this house. Only certain farmers, not all, can come under that act. But why should one department of government say, " Go to another department and get redress; we are not going to do anything for you." I say the principle is not sound, and it should not be tolerated. When the minister rises, I want him to tell us just what that office in British Columbia will cost to maintain. I have given the total collections of last year, and without knowing the exact figures I maintain that it will cost close to $100,000 to maintain the thirteen supervisors plus the staff in that office. If this amendment goes through, as I see the minister intends it to, it will mean that very little if any money will be collected. Let me repeat, that out of 1,668 settlers under the board only 475 paid up in full. I maintain that those figures speak for themselves and show a serious condition prevailing in the Fraser valley among the soldier settlers.
I make one last urgent plea to the minister to reconsider this question very carefully and seriously before these amendments are passed. They may be all right for Saskatchewan or Alberta or Manitoba, but for British Columbia the result is going to be tragic indeed.

speechtext:
I wish to associate myself as strongly as I can with what has been said by the two hon. members who have preceded me. I believe there is one further point I might contribute to this debate; that is the question of discrimination. The minister must realize that when this act was passed 51952-98
conditions were very bad, and one of the reasons it was passed was to help soldier settlers at that time. Fortunately, in some parts of the country conditions have become a little bit better. The price of wheat has increased, and there are now some soldier settlers who could avail themselves of the opportunity offered under this legislation, if it were allowed to be extended until 1941, to operate in exactly the same way as it has been operating up to the present time.
Furthermore, I say discrimination has been shown because those who might have been able to avail themselves of this legislation in the past might have been living in the dried-out areas. Possibly they have not had any crops. If conditions should change, as the fond hope of the Minister of Agriculture as . expressed from time to time would lead us to believe, these people would be in a position to avail themselves of this legislation. Furthermore, it would be to the advantage of all concerned in Canada if the government were to set an example by effecting rearrangements along this line.
May I point out to the minister that a problem very similar to this one, respecting school lands, existed in certain provinces. School lands had been sold at a time when land was very high, and it was found during the years of the depression that due to the drop in the prices of farm products it was impossible for the purchaser to meet the payments due upon those lands. The matter was taken up by the various provincial governments. I know in one particular case a board was appointed to investigate the question, and as a result drastic reductions were made.
I believe the example the government is setting in this legislation is not a good one, and I suggest that the minister consider seriously before he presses passage of the bill. So far as I am concerned, I can only oppose it. I believe the minister has heard enough argument, not to make him change his mind but possibly to provide him with more information than he had when the legislation was first introduced. I believe he might very well reconsider the passage of the bill.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni has read a letter from the Soldiers Settlers' Union with headquarters at Lloyd-minster. I have a copy of that letter and, living within thirty miles of that particular headquarters I feel I should be remiss in my duty were I not to uphold the request contained therein. I have known the conditions there for a number of years. Speaking some time ago to the committee, I gave

Soldier Settlement Act

figures showing that during the years 1931 to 1937 inclusive, soldier settlers reduced their indebtedness to the extent of $40 or at the rate of $6 a year.
May I point out that those settlers were not able to provide a living for their families such as is enjoyed by hon. members now sitting in this committee. If hon. members who have had the opportunity to stay at the large hotels at Winnipeg, Saskatoon, Edmonton and Vancouver believe that the soldier settlers enjoy the kind of living obtained at those hotels, I would ask them to go out among the farmer settlers, have a meal there and sleep a night or two in their homes. After doing that, those members might have a little more information about the conditions under which the settlers are living.
So far as saving money is concerned, I do not think the minister and the government have been fair to the settlers. The figures show that every year this oppression has continued; that the settlers are suffering more and more, and that the country is losing more and more money. I believe the government is in possession of all the facts and figures, and further debate would be a waste of time. I suggest, however, that the government would be well advised to take drastic steps to give the soldier settlers a chance to get possession of their homes, and that no more time should be wasted.
Mr. O'NEILL:	Mr. Chairman, I have
received numerous letters and communications from farmers in my district, with reference to this bill, requesting me to use my influence- if I have any-with the government to have the bonus privilege extended another three years, or until 1941. I have on my file one letter from a farmer who wrote expressing his appreciation of the bonus period having been extended. Apparently he took it for granted, from the Hansard report, that the bonus privilege was to be extended to 1941. A number of members have taken that meaning from the resolution, and a number of farmers throughout Canada took the same meaning from it. I have only one letter expressing appreciation of the action being taken by the government, but have numerous letters asking that we take that attitude. I do not know what the minister intends to do, but I should like to add my voice to those of the hon. members for New Westminster, Comox-Alberni and other constituencies who have spoken in favour of the amendment to the bill, and have asked that it be extended to everybody until 1941, the same as it has been since 1933.

subtopic: INTEREST RATE ON REPAYMENTS OF TAXES AND INSURANCE PREMIUMS-ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to trespass upon the time of the committee, having urged as strongly as I can the desirability of continuing the present scheme for another two or three years. I indicated to the minister the reasons which had induced my government to take the position it did take. A number of those concerned were brought to Ottawa and conferences were held. As a result of careful consideration it was concluded that this method would be the best one to clear up the situation.
From time to time we have written off large sums of money. The mere writing of that off means that we have lost that much money without doing the settler any very great good, except to lessen the amount which he has to pay. And it is agreed that he cannot possibly be in a position, at any time within the vision of the ordinary mortal, to pay off the obligations as originally created. That being so, there were two methods only by which the matter could be dealt with: One was writing off the obligations, which we did, and the other was to create some condition which would be an incentive to the settler to want to get title to his property. And it was believed-I am bound to say the result justified the belief-that if we gave him credit for two dollars for every one dollar he paid he would be most anxious to pay up the balance due and secure title to his property.
We now have evidence from the hon. member for New Westminster that conditions have been so hard in that locality that payments have been very few. Then, we have heard evidence from the hon. member for Comox-Albemi as to what conditions have been out there. The hon. member for Kamloops has given his views, and hon. members from the prairies have spoken. Yesterday I received a telegram from central Alberta repeating the considered opinion of a large number of settlers that the effect of this inducement which is offered by statute to those who are on the lands, had been excellent, and hoping that the inducement would be continued.
I quite understand the position taken by the minister, but I cannot understand how he expects to get more money by pursuing the method suggested in the bill. If money is to be obtained, then in some way you will have to change the old saying: You cannot get blood from a stone. From no part of the house has a member risen and stated that there was ability to pay on the part of the settler; there is no suggestion anywhere that he has had the ability to pay but would

Soldier Settlement Act
not pay. There is no indication that in any manner whatsoever he has endeavoured to disregard his obligations. On the contrary, according to the evidence given by the minister a few evenings ago, four million dollars have come into the exchequer under the operations of this scheme. Putting it on the lowest possible level, that of the exchequer itself, I cannot think that we could receive as much money by any method different from that which we have adopted here, namely, to create such inducement on the part of the settler to want to pay that when he pays one dollar he gets credit for two. I do not suggest that that be continued forever, but we should try it for at least two or three more years.
Have conditions improved so greatly in this country? Why do I make that suggestion? We are just beginning to realize the true conditions. We are just beginning to realize that what we spoke of as a great movement forward was in fact no such thing. We are now beginning to feel the effects of the great recession that has taken place in the United States. According to the figures brought down the other day, our exports last month to the United States were not one-half of what they were a year ago. They are $17,000,000 as against $36,000,000. Under such conditions, is it fair to do what is proposed? Is it quite just? Is it quite in keeping with what we have done? Is it not an utter and entire disregard of the record of the past, of what we have done in writing down and providing inducements with regard to payments? How can people pay anything under the economic conditions that have been mentioned in the debate of to-day and a few evenings 'ago? These people are just keeping body and soul together.
I do not want to speak of my own personal experiences, but I have guaranteed the obligations of many of these men. I suppose there is no harm in my saying that the other day I sent a cheque for $4,000 to a bank in connection with a guarantee I had given for one of these soldier settlers. He was there with his little family and he could not get about very well as the children were quite young. What are we going to say in the face of this recession that is reflected so terribly in our exports? Are we going to say: Well, this is a good time to stop being friendly and kindly; the time, has now arrived when we want our dollar. I know the Minister of Mines and Resources is a kindly man, and I should like him to tell the committee what has induced the government to take this position. There has been no indication to this chamber
of what has happened. There is nothing a single hon. member can say in explanation of what has been done except that we want our money. It is a bad time to want it. I do not mind telling you that it is always a bad time to want money when you cannot get it. That is the position; we are not going to get it.
I do not want to prophesy, for the role of a prophet has never been one that conduces to longevity. If I remember rightly the teachings of holy writ, some prophets fell into rather evil days. I shall not endeavour to prophesy, but I venture to think that those hon. members who return next year and ask the minister how much money he has received under his new act will find themselves greatly disappointed. Why not let us be just, not generous? Why should we depart from tradition? I shall not put it as high as tradition; why should we depart from the past record, the record not of one government alone? Mark you, if this were political I would not be talking of it in this way; it is something more than that. Essentially it gets down to this:	Do we value keeping a man on the
land where he can try to work out a livelihood for himself and his wife and his children? Do we say that we do not? This bill says we are to say to him, "Pay or get out."
The hon. member for New Westminster says that it means the spending of thousands of dollars in British Columbia because we are going to maintain the machinery of large numbers of inspectors and others for the purpose of inspecting the inspectors and other work of that kind. I plead with the minister. I asked him to think it over the other evening, and that is all I could do. I am sure he has done that. Are we going to go back to our several peoples, get them together and say: "Well, boys the government has concluded that you are so well to do, so happy and contented, that you will want to pay up, plus interest at five per cent; they have changed the order of things and provided that this is to be dealt with in a new way, namely, one hundred cents on the dollar and credit for just one hundred cents when you pay it. Look at what we have done." I am to tell my friends that we have reduced the interest rate from seven to five per cent. I am to tell them that we have cancelled the arrangement whereby they received credit for two dollars for every one that was paid. I must tell them that we are now going to ask them to pay one hundred cents on their obligation.
It cannot be done and it will not be done. Why not let us take the matter courageously in hand and say that we shall continue with
Soldier Settlement Act

the old plan; that we shall give them another couple of years of it? If it works out, all right; if it does not work out, so much the worse, we shall have to do something more. That is all I suggest to the minister. I apologize for trespassing again upon the time of the committee. If it were not that I felt so strongly about this matter, I would not urge it with such pertinacity and persistence. But I feel strongly about it, and I believe beyond peradventure in the suggestions which we make. These are not political suggestions; they are suggestions that come from observation, from experience and from some little knowledge of under just what conditions these men are living and of the effort they are making to be honest, decent citizens with an earnest desire to meet their obligations. But this they cannot do under existing economic conditions.

subtopic: INTEREST RATE ON REPAYMENTS OF TAXES AND INSURANCE PREMIUMS-ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I disagree somewhat with the right hon. leader of the opposition. The only soldier settler who will not get any benefit under this legislation is the settler who has completed all his payments up to March 31 of this year and who has consequently taken full advantage of the bonus. Let that be clearly understood. I almost thought that the leader of the opposition was under a misapprehension. When this legislation was passed in 1933 establishing the principle of a dollar for dollar bonus, it was given a life of only three years. At that time the price of practically everything produced on a soldier settler farm was at the lowest point in the history of this country. If the situation is so desperate now when prices have doubled, according to the price index, why did the government of the day not make this applicable for five or ten years? They evidently contemplated at that time that there should be a limit, and in the law they passed they imposed a limit of three years. Later, in 1936, it was thought .advisable to extend the privilege for another period. As I have stated before, legislation was introduced in this house extending it for a period of three years, but in another place that period was reduced to two years.
The criticism I would make of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni-and the same thing applies to the hon. member for New Westminster-is that they take a few cases, perhaps a number of cases, in British Columbia where conditions are bad, and then reason from that that this proposal should apply right across Canada. There are returned soldiers who have taken advantage of the dollar for dollar privilege, and who are in a position to complete their payments on their

land; yet in order to confer an advantage on a returned soldier settler in Comox-Alberni my hon. friend proposes to extend this privilege right across the board to people who would no doubt be very glad to take advantage of it, but who on a basis of equity really do not need it. I am sometimes surprised in this house at the easy way in which we deal with obligations owing to the government.
As I said before, I am not now going to criticize the inauguration of this scheme about twenty years ago; but I venture to say that before the country is through with the soldier settlement experiment, it will have cost the country anywhere from $75,000,000 to $100,000,000, and probably nearer the latter figure.

There is no one in this chamber who is more desirous of dealing fairly with the returned soldiers than I am. I know the sacrifices these men made for their country. Some have, perhaps in a moment of misguided zeal, gone on farms, many of them not equipped with the necessary experience and knowledge to succeed in that vocation.
I repeat what I said before, that this legislation is, I think, fair. There is a way of dealing with the extreme cases to which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has referred, and I say this, that the soldier settlement board administration will facilitate in every way the cases of those who are in the plight referred to by him and by the hon. member for New Westminster before a tribunal where all the facts can be made known and an adjustment be arrived at. The soldier settlement board administration will not put anything in the way of that adjustment; we will facilitate it in every way.

No; my hon. friend is, I
am afraid, again overstating the case.
What are the advantages of that method? The advantages it seems to me are these, that the individual soldier settler can go before what is in effect a court where he can be certain of the fairest kind of treatment, and the soldier settlement . board administration is not going to put any obstacle in his way. Individual cases can be dealt with in that fashion. The man who is not entitled to consideration will not get it from the board, but the man who is entitled to consideration

Soldier Settlement Act
will get it. It seems to me that this is a much more equitable and fair way of dealing with this problem than for us in a great burst of generosity in this house simply to say: We are going to extend this privilege right across Canada, from Halifax to Vancouver, to everyone whether he needs it or not.
There are many who have taken advantage of this privilege. One would almost imagine, listening to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, that no one in British Columbia had been able to take advantage of this legislation. As a matter of fact, in the Vancouver district-and that includes, I think, all of British Columbia-there were still 1,312 soldier settlers on land at the 31st of December, 1937; of that number 1,165 had been able in some degree to take advantage of the dollar for dollar privilege which has been in effect for the past five years. I cannot at the moment give the precise extent to which they have been able to take advantage of it, but I submit that the picture is not nearly so black as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni pictures it, or as bad even as my good Scotch friend from New Westminster pictures it, when 1,165 soldier settlers out of 1,312 in British Columbia have been able in some degree to take advantage of the bonus.
I repeat, there is the machinery to adjust individual cases. It is not necessary, in order to deal with a few hundred or perhaps even a larger number of cases in British Columbia, to pass legislation that will be effective right across Canada and give advantages to those who, so far as I am aware, are not asking for it and probably do not need it. I think at times we should give some consideration to the position of the taxpayers of this country. I believe the great majority of the returned soldiers do not want to be unfair or unreasonable. They do not wish to get at the expense of the taxpayer something to which they are not entitled.
I admit that this question is a difficult one to deal with. I know I shall probably be misrepresented from one end of the country to the other in bringing down this legislation, but nevertheless I submit it is fair and reasonable. If economic conditions change within the next year or two and the situation comes that the right hon. leader of the opposition came near prophesying, it will always be open to parliament to reconsider its decision. It is not a closed book, if conditions change to warrant reconsideration by parliament.

If within a year or two from now the economic situation has changed and prices come down, it is always open to parliament to reconsider the legislation. I think it is quite clear that when the legislation was first introduced and made effective for only three years, it was brought down to meet an extraordinary economic situation in this country. Notwithstanding the predictions of my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition, the situation to-day is vastly better than it was then, and I think we can well afford to accept this legislation, and if necessary review the situation a year or two years from now.

' Mr. COLDWELL:	Speaking in round
figures, as the minister has been doing, one is apt to give an entirely exaggerated picture of what has happened. If the minister had told the committee as well what number of cancellations had been made and the number of quit claims that have been given over the same period, I think it would show that the soldier settlers have not been able to do very much. I agree with what has been said in this discussion. The letter just read by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and referred to by the hon. member for Battle River has also reached me and I would draw the minister's attention to the last paragraph. We strongly urge that a conference be arranged to bring about a permanent solution to the settlement problem.

I believe that one of the causes of dissatisfaction among the soldier settlers is the feeling that in recent years they have not been able to have a conference with the minister to discuss the matter. I shall not enter into the controversy that has been raised regarding the legion resolution. I believe the legion passed that resolution in good faith on information which it had. But it was pointed out that certain representatives of the settlers were not able to be present. I am very sorry indeed that the government has not seen fit to extend the bonus. I was puzzled until a few minutes ago, when I heard the minister's statement, as to why they would not continue the bonus. It appears from the statement of the minister that his sole reason is the protection of the taxpayers of the country. He has referred to large sums that have been paid, though I am not sure whether he mentioned British Columbia. At any rate, large sums have been paid into the treasury. Has he any idea how much of that would not have been paid if we did not have the bonus? There would have been very little as far as British Columbia is concerned, and I believe the minister will find at the end of the year that cutting out the bonus will result in lower collections. His collections will drop considerably add in some parts of Canada they will drop out of sight. I do not suppose there is any use in continuing this debate and pointing out objections. I have received a number of letters of protest from British Columbia. I have al?o a telegram from the Canadian Legion from Haney, British Columbia, dated March 14, addressed to myself:
Strongly urge you support amendment bonus scheme. Failure secure this extension will dishearten many struggling to make good this district.
That is signed by the president of the Canadian Legion, branch 88. From the figures the minister has given, it appears that there were 147 in the province who did not take advantage of this legislation. Therefore, if this amendment goes through to-night, it means that the only men for whom provision will be made will be these 147.

I may be wrong, but I thought the minister said that there were 1,165 who had taken full advantage of it. At any rate there is a large number of those who have been unable to pay during the last few years, and they will certainly not be able to pay in the next three years. I know that a large number of those who have been paying will become discouraged and make no payments at all. It is all right to say that they can go to the farmers' creditors arrangement board, but these men are not bankrupt. An odd one may be, but a man who has been struggling along and making his payments in order to get that extra amount credited cannot go to that board the next year or the year following. He will not be bankrupt.
Back in 1933 when this legislation was first introduced, we know the condition. It was supposed to be temporary. At that time we thought that we should be back in prosperous times within three years. At any rate it was going to be easy to extend the term. It was extended; but according to the prices of farm products quoted here to-night, conditions are not very bright in many parts of this country to-day, and there is little opportunity for these returned soldiers on the land to make even fifty per cent of their payments. The minister infers that the soldier settlers in eastern Canada are in fairly good condition. I do not know about that, but I know how they are in British Columbia. In 1933, when this legislation was first introduced, we found some soldier settlers owing on their land perhaps $5,000. One in particular pointed out to me that he could go across the road and buy an identical piece, with the same acreage, for S3,000. I said, "For goodness sake buy it, and throw up your place." He said, "Well, there is this bonus; if I can keep on paying, with that bonus I shall be able to clear this place for a total payment of $2,500, with of course, interest added." Many of them viewed the matter in that light, that with the bonus it gave them a revaluation of their land, and they were encouraged to stay on and try to complete the payment.
Another suggestion was made the other evening by my leader in regard to the rate of interest, which I understood the minister was going to take into further consideration. They reduced the rate to five per cent; I thought it might be reduced to at least four per cent. Speaking of interest, I took up with the Minister of Finance the other day
a little question of interest. There is in British Columbia a firm of which a number of the employees are returned soldiers. They decided to enter into a scheme by which their savings might be set aside and saved for their old age or for some future date. The question arose how to invest those savings. They said to me that in the post office savings bank they could get only two per cent. I took the matter up with the Minister of Finance, and this is what he said:
I might say, however, that if the operations of the fund are such as to require that they should he available for withdrawal in cash form at any time, then in view of the current situation with respect to interest allowable on notice deposits or on short-term loans it would appear that two per cent is not an unreasonably low rate of return. I might mention, for example, that the dominion government is currently obtaining short-term funds for just over one-half of one per cent.
These returned men can obtain two per cent on their money; according to the Minister of Finance that is about the limit; but soldier settlers are called upon to pay five per cent.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT

speechtext:
Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport) moved the second reading of Bill No. 31, to establish a board of transport commissioners for Canada, with authority in respect of transport by railways, ships and aircraft.
Transport Commission

He said: Mr. Speaker, the object of this bill is to promote the stabilization of the transport industry in Canada, in the public interest as well as in the interests of all those engaged in transportation. The bill extends regulation of rates to inland shipping and to 1 commercial air transport.
No one questions the benefit of the government regulation as applied to the railways, least of all the railways themselves. The government believes that the extension of rate regulation to our inland waterways and to our commercial airways will carry with it similar benefits.,/ It should be made clear from the first that there is no intention to limit development on sound economic lines of any form of transportation in favour of any other form of transportation. It is inevitable that the development of newer forms of transport will be accompanied foy some loss of business from older forms of transport, and it is not the purpose of this bill to interfere with that process, so long as the same rules of competition apply to all. j
The purpose of the government is to bring about a situation where competition may make for the benefit of the public and health within the industry. We all recognize that Canada must have an adequate railway service, since without it and for climatic and geographic reasons it would be impossible to conduct the business of the nation. We also recognize that our great inland waterway must be served by transportation agencies conducted on a sound economic basis, so that these waterways may continue to provide those low-cost transportation facilities that make it possible for our western farmers to compete in the markets of the world.
Transportation by air is still in its infancy, and it is logical that the development of this industry should be conducted along sound lines, under government regulation. It is a matter of public interest that transportation rates be reasonably stable, and applied without discrimination. Experience has shown that publicity is essential to prevent discrimination. Therefore the publicity of rates is a fundamental requirement in this bill.
We also appreciate that our transportation rate structure may break down completely unless some relation is maintained between transportation charges and the abilities of various commodities to stand those charges. There is also the problem of conditions of employment in transportation industries. It will not be a question that it is the duty and' interest of all employers to endeavour to maintain reasonable standards of conditions
[Mr Howe.l
and rewards of employment. The absence of regulation and the resulting uneconomical competition must inevitably bear heavily on the workers, since labour costs comprise such a large proportion of operating expenses. The wide difference in working conditions, as between regulated transportation and unregulated transportation, must be apparent to all. Apart from the effect on labour, the interest of public safety is also involved.
Objections to this bill have taken the form, not that regulation is undesirable, but rather that the means provided by the bill may work hardship in certain specific instances. Many have objected on the ground that the bill will have the effect of increasing rates. I see nothing in the bill which can reasonably lead to that conclusion. The fact is that Canadian railway rates, as established under regulation, are among the lowest in the world, and this has been accomplished notwithstanding the fact that Canada is a sparsely populated country. Regulation should have the effect of lowering rather than raising rates, by tending to eliminate wasteful and destructive competition among the various forms of transportation.
It has been assumed that under this bill the transport commission will fix rates. That is not the purpose of the bill. It provides, rather, for policing the methods of. rate fixing used by the transportation companies themselves, in order to substitute order for chaos, and to ensure the elimination of unjust discrimination between one shipper or passenger and another shipper or passenger.

speechtext:
On the other hand, individual carriers who fear that rate regulation will result in the establishment of unreasonably low rates, as a result of the board of transport forcing carriers to adopt the lowest rate published by an improvident competitor, can be assured that the bill provides ample remedies against such a condition. There is

Transport Commission
nothing in this bill which can be used to force carriers to furnish services at rates that cannot be economically justified.
There was a time when transportation in Canada was largely a railway monopoly, without state regulation of rates. The need for regulation at that time was apparent to all. In 1888 the railway committee of the privy council was given certain powers of rate regulation. This seemed to satisfy the public until about 1898, when there was an insistent demand for adequate regulation. After extended government investigation, the Railway Act was amended, in 1903, to provide for the organization of a railway commission. The board was established in 1904 with very wide powers over railways constructed under federal authority, as well as over railways constructed by provincial authority, when such railways are declared by the parliament of Canada to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. The first membership of the board was restricted to three commissioners; but four years later, 1908, when our railway mileage was approximately 25,000 miles, three more commissioners were added, and the usefulness of the board increased by an arrangement permitting the board to be divided into two sections, each of which could sit independently, the decision of either section being, under the act, the decision of the board.
When the board of railway commissioners was first established, the railway exercised a virtual monopoly in the field of transport. The competition from inland waterways was negligible; the automobile was a novelty, and the aeroplane was a thing of the future.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: There was always water competition on the great lakes, was there not?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Yes, but at that time it was not a serious competitor with the railways, because it was confined almost entirely to bulk cargoes. The railways no longer enjoy a monopoly in the field of transportation. The rapid development of the internal combustion engine and its application to trucks, buses and automobiles, and the constant demand for paved highways, have brought highway transportation very prominently into the transportation picture. It is unnecessary for me to remind hon. gentlemen of the effect of highway competition upon railway revenues.
The construction of the Welland ship canal has also had a marked effect upon transportation problems, in that it has created a surplus of boats of the type that formerly confined their operations between Port Col-borne and Montreal. These boats have now
extended their operations to the head of lake Superior, and to obtain cargoes have made serious inroads into the package freight business formerly carried by the railways. The fact that the railways are subject to regulation while the motor vehicles and water carriers are not, has placed a severe handicap on the ability of our railways to meet this new competition. On the other hand, lack of regulation has not brought prosperity to the unregulated carriers. Competition has been of the destructive type, not only to the railway earnings but to the earnings of its new competitors.
Both the railways and the public have no doubt that regulation has been beneficial to railway transportation. There is every reason to believe that the extension of regulation to other forms of transportation would have been demanded by the public before this, were it not for the fact that the railways themselves are now in effect the regulators for competing forms of transportation. Railway rates are published, and generally represent the maximum that competing agencies can demand, while unregulated transportation can underbid the railway to such an extent as may be necessary to divert business from the railway. The public have the railway to fall back on when other forms of transportation disappear, and so have not become alarmed at the destructive effect of the competition from transportation that is often of the "fly by night" variety. In short, the railway tariffs form a protective blanket over the rates of competitors to the railways. A reduction in railway rates to hold railway business can have no permanent effect, other than to drive some of its competitors to more profitable fields.
Canada is practically the last country to apply state regulation to transportation other than railways. The United States have extended the authority of the interstate commerce commission to all railway operations, pipe lines and motor vehicles operating across state boundaries. Its Motor Carrier Act of 1935 has done much to regulate commercial vehicles on the highways and to coordinate highway rates with railway rates. Similarly, United States coastwise ocean traffic is regulated, as well as coastal carriers operating between ports on the Atlantic and ports on the Pacific through the Panama canal. Regulation has not as yet been applied to inland waterways, such as the great lakes and the Mississippi river; but there has been introduced in the senate by the chairman of the senate committee on interstate commerce, a
Transport Commission

bill which will provide, through the interstate commerce commission, the same or even more extensive regulation of shipping on the great lakes than we propose under this bill.

speechtext:

j which was up last year?
i Mr. HOWE: Yes; it was not reached. In Great Britain, state regulation is exercised over the railway carrier, the highway carrier and the water carrier. The same situation exists in northern Ireland.
In the Union of South Africa, the state owns all railways and exercises complete control over highway vehicles for hire for passengers and goods. A scale of charges must be filed with the regulating body, and the reasonableness of those charges is decided by the board. In New Zealand and Australia, the regulating bodies have control over all forms of transportation, and a certificate of convenience and necessity is necessary before any new carrier can operate. It will thus be observed that Canada has been slow to accept a situation that most other countries have dealt with.
This bill applies regulation to shipping other than for bulk cargoes, such as wheat, iron ore and raw materials, that are handled in bulk without packaging. The reason for excluding bulk cargoes is that these are not competitive, being carried at rates so low as not to be attractive to rail carriers. In my opinion, both the public and the carriers would benefit by the extension of regulation to bulk carriers; but as a number of protests were received when this bill was considered previously, the government has decided to exclude bulk carriers from the bill. Regulation j of shipping applies only to rates, as safety i features are now regulated by the shipping act. ! Transportation by air is a comparatively new industry and, therefore, regulation can be applied without any serious dislocation. It is believed that regulation is generally acceptable, both to the operators and to the public. Regulation under this bill applies only to aircraft operating on regular schedules, over regular routes. It does not apply to carriers engaged in pioneer work or on casual services.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Or a private undertaking.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
No; this applies only to public carriers. Provision for agreed charges extends to the railways a privilege that is now enjoyed by highway carriers, water carriers and aircraft, that of contracting with a shipper to handle his shipments exclusively at a rate which may be lower than the tariff rate. Agreed charges are now a well established

feature of British transportation and have proved beneficial both to the carriers and to the shipper. The principle has also been generally adopted in France. In short, the principle of agreed charges permits a earner to give to a shipper who gives all his business to the carrier a lower rate than must be given to another shipper who prefers to pick and choose between various types of carriers.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Is there any such thing
on any other part of this continent?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
It has not been applied on this continent; but it has been applied in England for about three years, and I have been told it has proven to be quite beneficial.
The bill provides for full publicity of rates granted under agreed charges, and provides against discrimination as between shippers who wish to obtain the benefit of agreed charges. There can be no discrimination as between the large shipper and the small shipper. In fact, the principle of the agreed charges works to the benefit of the small shipper, who cannot always obtain as low a rate for highway transportation as can his larger competitor.
The fairness of a low rate for all year round shippers is obvious. In many sections of Canada, where the highways cannot be kept open the year round, everyone must use the railway for winter shipments. The agreed charge simply provides that in such cases, those shippers who agree to ship all year by railway will get an all year round rate, but those who elect to use the railway in winter and trucks in summer will not get the same treatment. It is a realistic treatment of a new development. There can be no harmful discrimination when it is provided that any shipper, big or small, who is willing to conform to the same terms, shall get the same treatment.
In my opinion the agreed charge presents a greater chance of preserving the low rate on long distance and bulk commodities, so essential to our national economy, and of putting a stop to the gradual withering of our rail service on many branch lines, the loss of which is an economic loss to the country, than any other measure of which I have knowledge. It is well worth a trial. It will tend to curb the uneconomic expansion of highway traffic and, by doing so, will afford an opportunity for the sound coordination of the two types of transportation, each within its own economic sphere.
Much is being said currently in favour of drastic measures to be applied for the purpose of reducing the operating expenses of

Transport Commission
our railways. The discussion extends to abandonment of five thousand miles of light traffic line, merging of locomotive and repair shops, consolidation of terminals and similar measures which would leave a trail of destruction across Canada that would, in my opinion, far outweigh any consequent real reduction in operating expenses. I regret to say that when this bill was last considered, those parliamentarians who are now most vocal in advocating such extreme methods, were strongest in opposition to the provisions of this bill. It must be apparent to all that the provisions of this bill will benefit our transportation industry, without in any way curtailing the extent or efficiency of transportation service in any part of Canada.
I sincerely hope that, in considering this bill, parliament will be disposed to place less dependence upon destructive and drastic solutions for our railroad problem, and will give serious and favourable consideration to this constructive step toward improving the economy of Canadian transportation. We all desire to avoid an increase in railway rates in Canada similar to that recently adopted in the United States. The public concern over the plight of the carriers in that country, where about forty per cent of railway mileage is in receivership, may be judged by newspaper comment on recent rate increases, amounting to five per cent on raw materials and ten per cent on finished products. Most newspapers commented that the increase should have been greater.
Transportation in Canada has done much toward the building of our national economy. Through this bill we can give it a measure of protection and assistance without imposing any burden on the Canadian people. When this bill is examined in committee, I trust that trivial objections and unjustified fears and alarms will not be permitted to cloud the real merit of the measures contained in the bill.
In order that the bill may have the fullest possible consideration, after the second reading I shall move that the bill be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

But so far as direction by the transport board or the board of railway commissioners is concerned, personally I believe it is unthinkable that any order would be made to increase freight rates in this country. That is my conviction, for what it may be worth.
In some respects we in Canada are a very fortunate people. We are the only country in the world in which there has been a railway commissioner who prepared the legislation. He prepared the legislation and has sat continuously for a period of thirty years on the board. Doctor McLean prepared the original act under instructions from the late Hon. A. G. Blair, and his report is a matter of record; it will be found in the library. When the statute was passed, or shortly after, he was appointed to the board and he has been there ever since, so that we have had a sort of continuity that has really been of very great value to Canada. At any rate, that is my judgment, and I am speaking only from my own observation; for I used to appear before the board frequently. I believe that the continuance of Doctor McLean there did much to establish with respect to our
Transport Commission

board of railway commissioners a certain type of jurisprudence which has been of great value to the Canadian people. Just how the change will affect us I cannot see; for there is no very great change in principle between the freight rate structure that is to be set up under this statute an'd the one set up under the board. In either case, as I read it, it is essential that approval be given, either by the transport board or by the board of railway commissioners, as it is now, before the rate can become effective.
I recall having once been engaged in interesting litigation in respect of the necessity for publication and for making available to every shipper the freight rates charged by the carrier. In a particular case they quoted a figure that was less than the statutory rate. It was indicated that we should bring action to recover the balance, because we were occupying a statutory position. I am bound to say that the court found the means to render it a little hard to recover, although not without some difficulty, because a freight rate was regarded as much in the nature of a customs impost. When a rate had been approved by the board it occupied a position somewhat analogous to that of an ordinary customs tariff rate, and I cannot make a compromise about a tariff rate with the Minister of National Revenue. If by mistake I pay too little, there is a limit of time within which he can take action and recover the rest from me, notwithstanding that in good faith I paid what the agent or customs officer at the point of entry demanded.
Now I am being led into many by-paths; I apologize. I desire only to say that the general principle of regimentation as applied to transport by sea and air and rail is one that I am sure will commend itself to the people and should commend itself to parliament if the result is anything like what the minister hopes for. We all trust that his expectations may be met and his hopes realized. I think it will require a major surgical operation rather than an anaesthetic to bring about this result. While this may be a suitable anaesthetic, I am afraid it will not serve as the major operation which is essential for the purpose of bringing about, shai I say, health to the subject of the operation. I think the minister is well advised to refer the matter to the committee, and I trust that the public may have an opportunity to make such representations as it may desire, and that it will be made widely known, through Hansard and through the press, that public bodies may have an opportunity to make such representations as they

desire with respect to the legislation. I think probably the only phase of the bill that will meet with much discussion is part V which deals with agreed charges on the one hand, and possibly-I say possibly-difficulties that may arise in connection with trade between Canadian and United States ports, either coastwise or other.

speechtext:
I should like to congratulate the minister on his achievement. I have only a vague knowledge, but it is sufficient to appreciate the enormous work this bill has cost him and those associated with him.
I am sorry to have to take exception to one item. I suppose if it is legitimate to talk about what is in the bill, it is also legitimate to talk about what is not in the bill. I refer to part II, which deals with transport by water. Subsection 4 of section 10 provides that the minister may license ships and may state in the licence the ports between which they may carry goods and passengers, and the schedule of services which shall be maintained. I would have liked to see that amplified in regard to the schedule of services, because that is the only allusion in the whole bill to that feature, and it is a very important feature.
Then the bill goes on to deal with tolls, charges, special rates, etc., at considerable length. Then, having built up what we will hope will be a desirable condition, it somewhat reduces its usefulness by section 12, subsection 4:
The provisions of this part shall not apply in the case of the transport of goods in bulk:-'
That has been dealt with by both the minister and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). That will seriously detract from its usefulness, I think, but the part that I have more interest in is the next:
5. The provisions of this part shall not apply in the case of ships engaged in the transport of goods or passengers
(a) between ports or places in British Columbia.
As far as we in British Columbia are concerned, that of course entirely annihilates the whole purpose of the bill. And I gather that the next section does away with any application to the whole coastal trade on the Atlantic. So apparently this section is left applicable only to shipping on the great lakes. Perhaps one should not call it discrimination, or class legislation; but certainly it is special legislation, leaving out the two coasts, where, as far as British Columbia, at any rate, is concerned, we badly need it.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
It is regional legislation.

Transport Commission

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Yes; I suppose that is the word which should be used. It is badly needed in British Columbia, so much so that in 1935 I introduced a bill to amend the Railway Act, which followed substantially the same lines as the minister's bill, except that mine applied to the coastal waters of British Columbia, and dealt at a little further length with tolls and routes and ports of call. There is ample precedent for this, because ships which obtain a subsidy from the dominion government have to comply strictly with such regulations. Each contract with the Department of Trade and Commerce sets forth a schedule of the ports of call and frequency of service covered by such contract, as well as rates and tolls. So we find that the port of call, the itinerary and rates and tolls are fully under the control of the Minister of Trade and Commerce if he grants a subsidy, however small, to that particular line of ships.
Moreover, it is fully competent under the Railway Act, because section 358 of that act extends its provisions to traffic carried by water by a railway company. Curiously enough it is confined to traffic carried by a railway company and does not apply to traffic carried by a shipping company which is only a shipping company. But if the shipping company is owned by or subsidiary to a railway company, it applies. That provision has been in our law for some twenty-nine years. When my bill was introduced a howl went up, of course, from British Columbia. Always a howl goes up if you propose any remedial legislation of this kind. The same thing occurred when the railway board act was introduced, only much more so; the heavens were to fall; business was to be ruined. But the railway legislation went through and no one would think of repealing it to-day. I think the same thing would have happened if my bill had been allowed to go through. People who would have been controlled howled about it, and many who would not have been controlled lent their assistance merely out of friendship or were afraid of something happening that was not going to happen.
Exactly the same reasons exist now as existed then for regulation of coastwise shipping. Even in 1907, when section 358 of the Railway Act was passed, the need was at least partly admitted, because they said- and the terms are very wide-"We will fully regulate the terms of water traffic when the traffic is carried by the ships of a railway company." It seems to me that was unjust. Why discriminate against the railway company? Why put a railway company that owns a line of ships operating in British 51952-99
Columbia waters under a handicap in competition with another line of ships not owned by a railway company? All my bill proposed was to put them all on an even footing. And there was reason for it. I had bitter complaints of discrimination by some companies there. I do not mind going as far as to say that one company practically threatened me with what would happen if I went on with this legislation. There was more or less of a monopoly out there. Of course it was not called a monopoly; that would be illegal, but called a gentleman's agreement.
