speechtext:
Yes; I would rather use that term, because the other stinks in my nostrils in connection with orientals. But I shall not go into that; it is one thing which, when you try to put your finger on it you find it is not there. It is there nevertheless. This company keeps out of this particular place and the other company keeps out of that place. I am not so sure that even the Canadian National does not have a look in at some of these friendly understandings. Then these people who opposed my bill two years ago put a great many obstacles in its path. It was going to apply, they said, to tugboats and every little launch that went to tow a boom of logs. That was all nonsense. It was not intended to do any such thing. I had made a mistake in the bill I drew, however; apparently it would have applied to ships going from the Pacific side to the Atlantic side; so in introducing the bill I explained that point and said I would be willing to accept an amendment providing that it would be applicable only to coastwise shipping as regards the Atlantic and Pacific; that it would not affect the traffic going from one coast to the other.
I know of cases of discrimination, some of which I have under my hand and could read, but I shall not detain the house. I am sure the minister has a copy of one letter, in which the writer said:
We have been following with interest in the newspapers whatever comment they printed on the new ministry of transport, and note that certain interests in Vancouver are objecting to certain coastal routes coming under the jurisdiction of the new ministry. It seems to us here that it would be a very good thing for us .	.	. rates both for passengers and
freight on this route, where they have no competition, are outrageous. We pay 65 cents minimum for 100 pounds of freight-the rate to Rivers Inlet is only 55 cents. We are roughly 130 miles from Vancouver, and our passenger rate is $6.50-five cents a mile.
I may mention that Rivers Inlet is 280 miles from Vancouver, while the place from

Transport Commission

which this man writes is only 120 miles. That is why I contend that some supervision is really required. It would not hurt the steamship companies eventually, because where political or other pull was brought to bear to force them to call at places where they were not justified in calling, they could appeal to the board and get relief, as the railways do now when they propose to close up a railway station or branch line on the ground that it is not profitable or necessary, and of course the people concerned raise an objection.
There is in British Columbia a place known as Howe Sound, no doubt called after some famous ancestor of the minister. Surely he will do the right thing by a place that has been named after his family. I think it was called after one of the captains or admirals on Vancouver's ships when they came to the Pacific coast. It is no longer in the district I represent, but at one time I did represent it. It is a place where there is a number of seaside resorts. A shipping company owned one of those resorts, and if you travelled on that line it is wonderful how easy and convenient it was to get off at that particular resort and how much more difficult it was to get off at a resort which was not owned by that company. I have even known a situation where the captain of the boat had an interest in a seaside resort. Again it was wonderful how much easier it was to get off at the right time and so on, at that place in which he had the interest, as compared with any other places.
I do not know what the situation is now, because that was a number of years ago, but I contend that there is ample reason for some provision of the kind I suggest. If the bill is not needed, as these people allege, no harm will be done, but it seems to be a case of the wicked fleeing when no man pursueth. If the thing is all right and needs no adjustment, no one will be any the worse off; but I say there is need for it and I do not know why the minister left that provision out of this bill. I am fairly certain that it was in the bill which was introduced in another place last year. Possibly, because of the difficulty of getting it through under adverse conditions, the minister has abandoned it. I will not say he has sold us down the river, but he seems to have abandoned that phase of his bill. I hope he will consider that point, because without it the bill is worth nothing to us. It is badly needed. It will not do any harm, and if we have a clause, as we have to-day in section 358 of the Railway Act, which makes it apply on the Pacific coast to the Canadian Pacific railway because they own a railway, is it not fair that it shall apply to other

competing companies which do not happen to own railways? It seems to me the logic is unanswerable. I wish the minister would consider that point before the bill goes to committee, to see if he could not do something along the lines I have indicated.

Mr. Speaker, before this bill proceeds further, I should like to point out with all due deference to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) that it would have been far better to repeal the Railway Act of 1919 and draw up a new act, because there is going to be a conflict between that act and this bill if it passes this house and the senate and receives the assent of His Excellency the Governor General.
The cardinal principle laid down in the Railway Act is that there shall be no discrimination. Under this act there may be discrimination, because the railway commission is empowered to permit shippers and those who transport goods either by rail or water to enter into agreements as to charges for a period of one year, or for a greater period. Therefore that rate may be different from the rates ordinarily laid down, and there would be an undue preference or discrimination which is not permitted under the Railway Act. That is the first objection I have to this bill. I believe there is going to be a conflict, because this legislation is to be administered by the railway commission, and is subject to the Railway Act. When you merge the two measures and the Railway Act is the one which controls, then any provisions of this measure which are in conflict with the Railway Act go by the board. That is quite clear.
One of the first provisions of this bill is that a licence shall be granted. Under the Railway Act there is no such thing as a licence. A transportation company has a right to transport goods. If it is an incorporated railway company it has a right to transport goods by rail. But the railway board fixes the rates, and if they are discriminatory or unfair or undue they go by the board. Under this bill, however, there is a licence granted by the transport commission. For instance, some of the things to be dealt with here are pulpwood, poles and logs, liquids, coal and coke, sandstone and gravel, ores and minerals, crude, screened, sized, refined or concentrated but not otherwise processed-

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN CANADIAN AND UNITED STATES GOVERNMENTS CONCERNING WATER DIVERSION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN CANADIAN AND UNITED STATES GOVERNMENTS CONCERNING WATER DIVERSION
speechtext:
On January 27, 1938, the Canadian government, through the agency of the Canadian minister to the United States, addressed a note to the United States government regarding the project of the Ontario government and the Hydro-Electric Power Commission to divert water from the Keno-gami river into lake Superior, this note being included in the white paper tabled on February 28, 1938. The reply of the United States government has now been received in the form of a note dated March 17, 1938, from their Secretary of State to the Canadian minister in Washington.
At the same time there has been received a memorandum also dated March 17, 1938, from the United States Department .of State, stating the views of the United States government on the importation of hydro-electric power from Canada, and allied questions. Both notes, and the memorandum, were delivered to the Canadian minister on March 18.
I beg leave to table copies of the communications from the United States government, as well as a copy of a letter of March 21 from the Prime Minister of Canada, to the premier of Ontario in this connection. The correspondence being tabled is being printed in a supplement to the white paper tabled in the House of Commons on February 28. It is expected that copies of this supplement to the white paper will be available for distribution to members of parliament by noon to-morrow. The correspondence is being translated at the

present time, and it is expected that the French text of the supplement will be available on Wednesday.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King, the house adjourned at 10.50 pm.
